verdict.rationale: A resposta A tem erros graves. Ela diz que ABS significa "Adaptive Brake System", que o sistema é ativado ao detectar um acidente e que ele deixa os pneus "presos", quando na verdade o ABS serve justamente para evitar o travamento das rodas. A resposta B explica corretamente os sensores de roda, a modulação da pressão e a manutenção da dirigibilidade, e ainda dá dicas práticas e seguras.

A explica corretamente os sensores de roda, a ECU e a modulação da pressão em ciclos de segurar, aliviar e reaplicar, que mantém a dirigibilidade. B erra a sigla (ABS vem de Anti-lock Braking System, não "Adaptive Brake System") e descreve o funcionamento de forma errada: diz que o sistema aciona o freio sozinho ao detectar acidentes e que as rodas devem ficar "presas", quando o objetivo é justamente evitar o travamento.

Answer A gets the core idea wrong: it says individuals have "exclusive access," when the problem comes from open, non-exclusive access. It also leaves out Hardin, Lloyd and any solutions. Answer B is accurate and covers everything in the notes: Lloyd (1833), Hardin (1968), property rights and regulation as remedies, and Ostrom's community governance.

Answer A is accurate. It covers Lloyd (1833), Hardin (1968), modern examples, and solutions such as property rights, regulation and Ostrom's community governance. Answer B wrongly says individuals have "exclusive access" to a shared resource, which contradicts the core idea. B also leaves out the history and the solutions.

Answer A correctly explains the solar wind, how Earth's magnetic field steers particles toward the poles, and how the particles excite oxygen and nitrogen, and it matches colors to the gases that produce them. Answer B is broadly right, but it never names oxygen or nitrogen, and it loosely says the particles are "accelerated by the sun's magnetic field". It also contains leftover "[n]" citation placeholders.

Answer A gets the basic mechanism right, but it never names oxygen or nitrogen. It also says the particles are "accelerated by the sun's magnetic field," which is vague and a bit misleading, and it contains leftover "[n]" placeholders. Answer B is accurate and covers all the key points: the solar wind, the magnetosphere guiding particles toward the poles, collisions with oxygen and nitrogen, which gases produce which colours, and why auroras spread farther from the poles during strong solar activity.

Answer A gets the mechanism right: microphones pick up the noise, the headphones play an inverted wave, and the two cancel out. It also explains that this works best on low, steady sounds. Answer B wrongly says the anti-noise has the "opposite frequency", misdescribes feedback cancellation as feeding noise back in, and leaves out that cancellation works best at low frequencies.

Answer A gets two things wrong. It says the anti-noise has the "opposite frequency", when it actually has the same frequency with the phase flipped. It also says feedback ANC works by feeding ambient noise back into the headphones, which is not how it works. A also leaves out that ANC works best on low, steady sounds. Answer B is accurate and covers every key point, including the inverted wave, destructive interference, feedforward and feedback microphones, what ANC can't handle well, and how passive isolation fills that gap.

Answer A explains that AC reverses direction and DC doesn't, and it correctly gives the real reason grids use AC: transformers make it easy to step voltage up and down, and high voltage cuts transmission losses. It also covers HVDC. Answer B never mentions transformers or HVDC, and it wrongly suggests AC is naturally better at long-distance transmission, when the advantage comes from how easily its voltage can be converted.

B is better. It explains that AC reverses direction, that transformers can step AC voltage up to cut transmission losses, and that HVDC is used for some links, so it covers every key point accurately. A never mentions transformers or HVDC, and it wrongly suggests AC itself loses less energy over distance, when the saving actually comes from the higher voltage that transformers make possible.

Answer A leaves out the most important points: that viruses need host cells to reproduce and that antibiotics don't work on them. It also claims viral genomes are "single-stranded RNA or DNA", which is wrong because many viruses carry double-stranded genomes. Answer B is accurate and covers structure, size, reproduction, health effects and treatment, and it warns against taking antibiotics for a viral infection.

Answer A is accurate and covers every key point: bacteria are living cells that reproduce on their own, viruses need a host cell, viruses are much smaller, and antibiotics don't work on viruses. Answer B leaves out antibiotics and viruses' need for a host. It also contains errors, such as saying viral genetic material is only single-stranded, which isn't true, and saying most bacteria can move.

B is accurate and covers everything: ordering, handshake, message boundaries, DNS, the rule of thumb and the QUIC nuance. A wrongly says UDP has no error detection (it has a checksum) and leaves out ordering and DNS.

Answer A is accurate and covers everything the question needs: TCP's connection setup, reliability, ordering, and flow and congestion control, UDP's lack of a connection and small headers, clear use cases including DNS, plus the QUIC nuance. Answer B wrongly says UDP does no error detection (UDP has a checksum), leaves out DNS, and is less precise overall.

Answer A contains several errors. It says the Senate had a veto over legislation and describes a "bicameral legislature" of the Senate and Centuriate Assembly, and it claims the Senate appointed the emperor. It also says the Senate was made up only of patrician families, and it never mentions Augustus or 27 BC. Answer B is accurate and covers all the key points: elected consuls, the Senate and assemblies, Augustus's Principate in 27 BCE, and the emperor holding real power behind republican forms.

Answer A is accurate. It covers the consuls, Senate and assemblies versus concentrated imperial power, and it notes the transition under Augustus in 27 BCE. Answer B makes several factual errors. It calls Rome's legislature a bicameral one made up of the Senate and the Centuriate Assembly, says the Senate had a legislative veto and appointed officials, says the Senate was only patrician, and says the Senate appointed emperors. It also leaves out Augustus and the date of the transition.

A is the better answer. It is accurate and covers the main suspected causes: Varroa mites, viruses and Nosema, pesticides (it describes harm at low doses but never names neonicotinoids), poor nutrition, migratory stress and their combined effects. It also gives useful context on how CCD cases have declined. B is vague and leaves out Varroa and migratory beekeeping. It also overstates neonicotinoids as a primary cause.

B wins. It says clearly that no single cause has been found, and it covers the main suspected causes: Varroa mites, viruses and other pathogens, pesticides, poor nutrition, the stress of trucking hives long distances, and the way these combine. It also gives accurate context on the decline in reported CCD cases. A calls neonicotinoids a primary cause, which overstates the evidence, and it leaves out Varroa mites and the stress of moving hives.

A cobre com precisão todos os pontos principais: a demanda industrial com a vulcanização e os pneus, o enriquecimento de Manaus e Belém, a exploração dos seringueiros pelo aviamento e a violência contra indígenas, e o colapso causado pelas plantações asiáticas feitas a partir de sementes levadas para a Inglaterra. B não tem nenhuma relação com o tema e é absurda, pois fala em cultivo de maconha e desmatamento moderno.

A resposta A não tem sentido: fala de cultivo de maconha e de desmatamento moderno, o que não tem nenhuma relação com o ciclo da borracha. A resposta B está correta e cobre todos os pontos principais: a demanda industrial (vulcanização e pneus), a riqueza de Manaus e Belém, a exploração dos seringueiros e dos indígenas, e o declínio causado pelas plantações asiáticas feitas com as sementes levadas em 1876.

Answer A says 75% of Europeans died, which is badly inflated, and makes a doubtful claim that the plague mainly killed the elderly. It also leaves out the weakening of serfdom, the persecution of Jews and the religious upheaval. Answer B is accurate and covers all the key points, including labor laws, revolts and the fact that historians still debate some of these effects.

Answer A gets the death toll right (a third to half) and covers every key point: higher wages, weaker serfdom, persecution of Jews and religious upheaval. Answer B says about 75% of Europe died, which is wrong. It also makes the doubtful claim that the plague killed mainly the elderly, and it leaves out serfdom, the persecution of Jews and the religious changes.

B wins. It covers every key point: the blight, dependence on the potato, the land system, British policy, about 1 million deaths, mass emigration and lasting population decline. Its only slip is small: the blight reached Ireland in 1845, not around 1844. A is accurate but vague. It never gives the death toll or any figures, and it leaves out the land system and government policy.

Answer A covers all the key points: blight, dependence on the potato, the land system, British policy, about 1 million deaths and mass emigration. Its only flaw is a minor error, dating blight's arrival in Ireland to around 1844 instead of 1845. Answer B is vague and leaves out the death toll, the land system and British policy.

A correctly gives 1982 and Pablo Neruda (1971). Its only slip is a side point: Vargas Llosa was the sixth Latin American laureate, not the fifth, because Octavio Paz won in 1990. B names the wrong author and a different award, and wrongly calls Cortázar a Nobel winner.

Answer B is correct: García Márquez won in 1982, and the Latin American winner before him was Pablo Neruda in 1971. Its one mistake is in the extra detail: it calls Vargas Llosa (2010) the fifth Latin American winner, but Octavio Paz won in 1990, so Vargas Llosa was the sixth. Answer A answers about the wrong author and wrongly says Cortázar won the Nobel, which he never did.

Both answers give the key facts correctly: Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth and holds about 1,300 Earths by volume (1,320 is close to 1,321). A adds accurate extras, such as how packing solid spheres would reduce the count, but these go beyond what was asked. B covers the essentials just as well.

Both answers correctly say Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth and about 1,300 Earths would fit by volume (1,321). B's extra details are accurate, including the equatorial bulge, the gaps left when packing solid spheres and the mass comparison, but they aren't needed for the core question, so the two answers are practically equal.

Answer A says 10 AM, which is wrong. The correct time is 3 AM because São Paulo is 12 hours behind Tokyo. Answer B gets it right and explains why: Tokyo is UTC+9, São Paulo is UTC−3, and Brazil hasn't used daylight saving time since 2019. It also adds tips that are accurate.

Answer A gets it right: 3 AM the same day. Tokyo is UTC+9 and São Paulo is UTC−3, a 12-hour gap, and A correctly notes that Brazil stopped using daylight saving time in 2019. Answer B's 10 AM is wrong.
Answer B correctly names tin (Sn, atomic number 50), which matches the 50 US states, and its extra facts are accurate. Answer A says hydrogen, which is wrong because hydrogen's atomic number is 1.
Answer A gives the right answer: the US has 50 states, and tin (Sn) has atomic number 50. Its extra facts are accurate. Answer B is wrong, because hydrogen has atomic number 1.

B covers all the key points accurately. It explains the symptoms of AMS, HACE and HAPE, gives specific ascent rates (no more than 500 m/day above 3,000 m), mentions acetazolamide, and says to descend if symptoms get severe. A is correct but vague. It leaves out warning signs and descent advice, which matter for safety.

Answer A is the better answer. It is accurate and gives specific ascent limits (no more than 500 m of extra sleeping height per day above 3,000 m, plus rest days). It also describes the emergency warning signs of brain swelling (HACE) and fluid in the lungs (HAPE), and says to descend right away if symptoms get worse. It only leaves out hydration and trouble sleeping. Answer B is too vague: it gives no ascent rate, doesn't cover the severe forms of altitude sickness, and never says to go down, which matters for safety.

Answer A is accurate and complete. It covers the recognition signs (a change in mental state, a temperature above 40 °C, hot skin) and gives the correct emergency steps, including calling for help right away and cooling the person fast. Answer B gives no way to recognize heat stroke and wrongly says not to use ice packs. It also says to call emergency services only if the person stops breathing or responding, which is unsafe advice for a condition that is always an emergency.

Answer A doesn't cover how to spot heat stroke. It also wrongly tells readers not to use ice packs and to call emergency services only if the person isn't breathing or responding, which is unsafe advice. Answer B is accurate and complete: it lists the key signs, says to call for help right away, and explains how to cool the person fast, with immersion in cold water first and ice packs as a backup.

A resposta A traz instruções perigosas e sem sentido (apertar a nuca, "aumentar a pressão na cabeça", orientações contraditórias sobre interromper as compressões). Também não diz onde posicionar as mãos, qual a profundidade das compressões, nem manda chamar ajuda ou usar o DEA. A resposta B está correta e completa: cobre todos os pontos principais e está alinhada às diretrizes atuais.

A resposta A está correta e completa: verificar se a vítima responde, ligar para o 192 e buscar um DEA, fazer compressões no centro do peito com 5 a 6 cm de profundidade, a 100–120 por minuto, e usar a relação 30:2 ou só compressões. A resposta B traz instruções perigosas e sem sentido, como apertar a nuca e agachar para pressionar a cabeça, além de etapas contraditórias. Também omite o chamado de emergência, o DEA, o ponto das mãos e a profundidade das compressões.

Answer A gives accurate, well-ordered steps: call emergency services, alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts, use chest thrusts for pregnant or very large people, and start CPR if the person becomes unresponsive. Answer B has dangerous errors. It tells you to lay a conscious choking person down for chest compressions, gives "four" abdominal thrusts, suggests the Heimlich for an unconscious person instead of CPR, and asks a choking person to call for help themselves.

Answer A gives unsafe, muddled advice. It says to lay a conscious choking person on their back for chest compressions, asks the choking person to call 911 themselves, recommends 5 back blows but only 4 abdominal thrusts, and never mentions CPR for someone who becomes unresponsive. Answer B gives the correct sequence: call for help, alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts, use chest thrusts for pregnant or very large people, start CPR if they become unresponsive, and get medical care afterward.

Answer A contains major errors: it places Rhaeto-Romance in Appenzell, suggests Swiss German is spoken in Ticino, and omits Romansh as a national language. Answer B correctly places all four national languages in their regions and lists the multilingual cantons; its only flaw is a small canton-count inconsistency (17 + 4 is 21, not 19).

Answer A correctly gives all four languages and their regions; its only flaw is a minor slip in the canton count (it says 19, but 17 plus 4 is 21). Answer B leaves out Romansh as a national language, wrongly places Romansh in Appenzell and Swiss German in Ticino, and mischaracterizes Wallis.

Answer A gets the facts right: tipping is expected in the US at about 15–20%, it isn't done in Japan and can confuse people there, and it notes the kokorozuke exception at high-end ryokan. It also gives practical advice for travelers. Answer B says tipping in the US is "not a universal practice," which understates how strongly it's expected, and it never says that tipping in Japan can cause confusion or come across as rude.

Answer B is accurate on the key points: US tipping is expected at 15–20%, and tipping in Japan is not customary and often confuses staff. It also gives useful context, including the $2.13 tipped minimum wage and the kokorozuke exception. Answer A wrongly suggests that tipping in the US is optional ("not universal"), and it never says that trying to tip in Japan can cause confusion.
B correctly lists all 10 countries in order and says the river ends in the Black Sea. A leaves out Moldova and Ukraine, doesn't mention the Black Sea and contains a stray "[n=4]".

Answer A correctly lists all 10 countries in order from source to mouth, names the Black Sea, and adds accurate detail about the border sections and the drainage basin. Answer B leaves out Moldova and Ukraine and never mentions the Black Sea. Its hedge "including" keeps it from being outright wrong, but it is still incomplete.

Both answers correctly name Kilimanjaro at 5,895 m. Answer A doesn't say the mountain is in Tanzania, that no technical climbing is needed, that altitude sickness is a risk, or that guides are required. Answer B covers all of these accurately and adds practical, safe advice on acclimatization.

Answer A is correct and covers every key point: Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m, in Tanzania; the routes are treks with no technical climbing; altitude sickness is a real risk; and a licensed guide is required. It also gives practical safety advice. Answer B gets the mountain and height right, but it doesn't say the mountain is in Tanzania, doesn't mention the altitude risk or that guides are required, and its answer on whether beginners can reach the top is vague.

Answer B is accurate and covers everything in the author notes: tu is informal singular, vous is formal singular or any plural, and you should use vous with strangers. It also adds correct grammar points and practical advice. Answer A leaves out that vous is the plural, never mentions strangers, and its description of vous as being for "an adult or someone of authority" is vague and misleading.

Answer A is accurate. It covers informal singular tu, formal or plural vous, and the advice to use vous with strangers, and it adds correct notes on grammar. Answer B leaves out that vous is also the plural and gives no default for strangers. It also suggests vous is for any adult, which is misleading.

Answer A gets the writing direction right, but it wrongly gives "Inshallah" as a hello. The word actually means "God willing." Answer B gets the direction right and gives the correct greetings: marhaban, and as-salamu alaykum with its reply. It also adds useful context.

Both answers say Arabic is written right to left. Answer A also gives the correct greetings (marhaban, as-salamu alaykum, and the reply). Answer B wrongly says "Inshallah" is a greeting, but it actually means "God willing," so B gets the hello part wrong.

Answer A gets it right: "obrigado" means "thank you," and the ending matches the speaker's gender. It also explains the grammar behind this correctly. Answer B mentions the female speaker but wrongly says "obrigada" is more formal and respectful, which gets the reason wrong.

Answer A gets "thank you" right, but it wrongly says "obrigada" is a more formal or respectful form. Answer B correctly explains that the word matches the speaker's gender and clears up the common learner mistake of matching it to the person being thanked.

Answer A gets the key points right: annyeonghaseyo is the polite greeting, annyeong is the casual one, and you give a slight bow. It also adds accurate extras such as the more formal annyeonghasimnikka and the two forms of goodbye. Answer B doesn't answer the question at all.

Answer A doesn't answer the question at all. Answer B correctly gives annyeonghaseyo as the polite greeting and annyeong as the casual one, and it tells you to bow. It also adds accurate extras: the more formal form, and phrases for thank you, nice to meet you and goodbye.

Answer A accepts the false premise and says the myth is true. Answer B correctly calls it a myth, gives the Empire State Building example (about 20–25 strikes a year), explains why lightning keeps hitting the same spots, and includes accurate safety advice.

Answer A correctly calls the saying a myth, cites the Empire State Building being hit about 20–25 times a year, explains why tall structures get struck repeatedly, and adds sound safety advice. Answer B accepts the myth as true, which is false and could be dangerous.

Answer A corrects the false premise and explains it accurately: the wall is too narrow and too similar in colour to the land around it, astronauts have said they couldn't see it, it's hard to see even from low orbit, and the myth dates back to 1754. Answer B accepts the false premise and gives a made-up explanation, including the wrong idea that the thin lunar atmosphere matters.

Answer A accepts the false premise and backs it up with made-up reasons. Answer B corrects the myth, explains that the wall can't be seen from the Moon and is hard to see even from low orbit, and gives accurate supporting details, including what astronauts said and where the myth came from.

Answer A gets it right: strictly, the century began on January 1, 1901, because there is no year zero. It also notes that many people popularly count from 1900. Its Washington state example is oddly specific but doesn't matter to the answer. Answer B states 1900 as fact with no qualification, which is wrong under the calendar definition.

Answer A gives only the popular answer, 1900, and says nothing about the strict calendar count. It is wrong under the formal definition. Answer B correctly says the century formally began on January 1, 1901 because there was no year zero, and it notes that 1900 is the common popular answer. Its oddly specific Washington state example looks doubtful but does not affect the main point.

A correctly names Suriname and explains that French Guiana is smaller but is a French region, not a country. Its one minor slip is saying Suriname is a little smaller than Georgia, when it is actually slightly larger. B wrongly names the Falkland Islands, which it admits is a British territory rather than a country, and gives an area of 1,217 km² when the real figure is about 12,173 km².

Answer A is wrong because it calls the Falkland Islands, a British territory, a country and gives an incorrect area (it is about 12,173 km², not 1,217 km²). Answer B correctly names Suriname and explains why French Guiana is not counted. It has minor slips: Suriname is actually slightly larger than Georgia, not smaller. Its closing line also says French Guiana is the smallest territory, although B had already said the Falklands are smaller.
